memory-intro-s1.title: Thinking about meaning and remembering words

study.introduction: Researchers tested whether the kind of question people answer about a word changes how well they remember it later.
study.participants: 90 adults (ages 18-60) recruited through a community library took part. All gave informed consent, and the consent form explained they could withdraw at any time.
study.method: Each participant saw the same 40 words, one at a time, and answered one yes-or-no question about each. A computer randomly assigned each participant to one of three conditions (30 per condition). Letters condition: "Is the word in capital letters?" Rhyme condition: "Does the word rhyme with train?" Meaning condition: "Would the word fit in the sentence She put the ___ on the table?" Participants were not told there would be a memory test. Twenty minutes later they were given a surprise test: a list of 80 words (the 40 they saw and 40 new ones), and they marked each word they had seen.
study.results: The letters group correctly marked 15% of the words they had seen, the rhyme group 45%, and the meaning group 78%.
study.discussion: Afterward, every participant was told why the test had been a surprise and could ask to have their data removed.

memory-intro-s2.title: Two tasks at once
memory-intro-s2.html: Forty students held a list of 7 spoken digits in mind for 20 seconds, then said them back. During the 20 seconds, every student did each of three things on different trials: nothing, repeating "the the the" out loud, or tapping a pattern on a keypad they could see. The table shows the percent of digits recalled in order.

table.caption: Percent of digits recalled in order, by what students did while holding the digits (invented data for practice)

items.q: Which concept do the results best support?
options: Levels of processing: thinking about meaning leads to better memory
Procedural memory: practicing a skill makes it automatic
Prospective memory: people remember planned actions better than words
Sensory memory: words held for a moment are fully stored

why.correct: The three questions differ in depth: letters (shallow, appearance), rhyme (sound), meaning (deep). Memory rose with depth, as the levels-of-processing idea predicts.
options: Right: The three questions differ in depth: letters (shallow, appearance), rhyme (sound), meaning (deep). Memory rose with depth, as the levels-of-processing idea predicts.
Procedural memory is for skills and habits. Marking words seen is explicit memory for facts, not a skill.
Prospective memory is remembering to do something in the future. No one had to remember to carry out an action.
Sensory memory lasts under a few seconds. The test came 20 minutes later and depended on how the words were processed.

items.q: How did this study operationally define memory for the words?
options: The type of question a participant answered about each word
The percent of seen words correctly marked on the 80-word list
How deeply a participant thought about the words while reading
The amount of time between seeing the words and the test

why.correct: An operational definition says exactly how this study measured the variable: correctly marked words on the surprise list, reported as a percent.
options: That is the independent variable, which the researchers assigned.
Right: An operational definition says exactly how this study measured the variable: correctly marked words on the surprise list, reported as a percent.
Depth of thought is the idea being tested. The study measured marked words, not thought directly.
The 20-minute delay was the same for everyone. It is a controlled detail, not the measure.

items.q: Each participant saw 40 words. On average, how many of those 40 words did the meaning group mark correctly?

why.correct: $78\%$ of $40$ words: $0.78 \times 40 = 31.2$, so about $31$ words on average (31 or 31.2 is accepted).

mistakes.why: 62.4 uses all 80 words on the test list. Only 40 of them had been seen, and the percent is of those 40.
78 is the percent, not a number of words. Take 78% of the 40 words seen.

items.q: The participants were not told about the memory test in advance. Which safeguard in the summary addresses this?
options: Random assignment: a computer placed each participant in one of the three conditions
Confidentiality: participants' names were removed from the data files
Debriefing: afterward each person learned why the test was a surprise
Animal care review: an animal welfare committee approved the procedure

why.correct: When a study withholds information, researchers explain the true purpose afterward (debriefing). The summary says this was done and data could be removed.
options: Random assignment is a design step that supports cause and effect, not an ethical safeguard.
The summary never mentions how names were handled.
Right: When a study withholds information, researchers explain the true purpose afterward (debriefing). The summary says this was done and data could be removed.
All participants were human adults, and no committee review is described.

items.q: Repeating "the the the" hurt digit recall much more than tapping a pattern. Which part of working memory best explains this?
options: The visuospatial sketchpad, which holds images and places
Long-term memory, which has a very large capacity
Sensory memory, which holds sounds for a few seconds
The phonological loop, which holds words and sounds

why.correct: Saying words out loud uses the same sound-based store that keeps spoken digits in mind, so the two tasks compete. Tapping uses the visuospatial sketchpad, which competes much less.
options: If the sketchpad held the digits, tapping a visual pattern would have hurt recall most. It hurt least.
The digits were held for only 20 seconds; the result is about what competes for space in the short-term store.
Echoic memory fades within seconds, long before the 20-second delay ended.
Right: Saying words out loud uses the same sound-based store that keeps spoken digits in mind, so the two tasks compete. Tapping uses the visuospatial sketchpad, which competes much less.

items.q: By how many percentage points was recall lower when repeating "the the the" than when doing nothing?

mistakes.why: 6 compares doing nothing with tapping. The question compares doing nothing with repeating words.
28 compares tapping with repeating. Compare repeating with doing nothing (86%).

items.q: Every student did all three tasks, on different trials. What is the main advantage of this design?
options: Each student is compared with themselves, so personal ability is held constant
It lets the researchers generalize the results to adults in many different cultures and settings
It turns the study into a correlational study of tasks and recall
It removes the need for an operational definition of recall

why.correct: When the same people do every condition, their individual abilities are the same across conditions, so a difference between conditions points to the task.
options: Right: When the same people do every condition, their individual abilities are the same across conditions, so a difference between conditions points to the task.
Generalizing depends on who the participants are (here, 40 students), not on doing every condition.
The researchers still set the tasks, so it remains an experiment; this design is one kind of experiment.
Recall still has to be measured exactly, here as the percent of digits said back in order.

items.q: Maya remembers her eighth birthday party, the cake and who was there. Which kind of memory is this?
options: Semantic memory
Episodic memory
Procedural memory
Prospective memory

why.correct: Memory of a specific personal event, tied to a time and place, is episodic memory, a kind of explicit memory.
options: Semantic memory holds general facts, like knowing what a birthday is, not a particular one you lived through.
Right: Memory of a specific personal event, tied to a time and place, is episodic memory, a kind of explicit memory.
Procedural memory is for skills, like riding a bike. Maya is recalling an event.
Prospective memory is remembering to do something later. Maya is remembering the past.

items.q: Ravi knows that Paris is the capital of France but cannot remember when or where he learned it. Which kind of memory holds this fact?
options: Episodic memory
Implicit memory
Semantic memory
Sensory memory

why.correct: General knowledge separated from the moment it was learned is semantic memory, a kind of explicit memory.
options: Episodic memory is tied to a particular personal event. Ravi cannot recall the event of learning it.
Implicit memory works without conscious recall, like a skill. Ravi can consciously state the fact.
Right: General knowledge separated from the moment it was learned is semantic memory, a kind of explicit memory.
Sensory memory lasts only a moment. This fact has lasted years.

items.q: Years after learning, Lena types quickly without thinking about where the keys are, but she cannot say where the letter G is without picturing a keyboard. Which kind of memory lets her type?
options: Semantic memory
Episodic memory
Prospective memory
Procedural memory

why.correct: Skills done without conscious recall are procedural memory, a kind of implicit memory. That is why she can type G but cannot easily say where it is.
options: Semantic memory holds facts you can state. Lena cannot easily state where G is, yet she types it.
Episodic memory is a personal event. Typing is a skill, not a remembered event.
Prospective memory is remembering to act in the future, like remembering to send a message.
Right: Skills done without conscious recall are procedural memory, a kind of implicit memory. That is why she can type G but cannot easily say where it is.

items.q: On his way home, Omar remembers that he promised to pick up bread. Which kind of memory is he using?
options: Prospective memory
Episodic memory of the promise
Procedural memory
Implicit memory

why.correct: Remembering to carry out an intended action in the future is prospective memory.
options: Right: Remembering to carry out an intended action in the future is prospective memory.
Episodic memory looks back at a past event. Omar is remembering a task still to do.
Procedural memory is a skill. Remembering an errand is not a skill.
Implicit memory works without awareness. Omar consciously remembers the plan.

items.q: A student walks out of a party and, without trying, knows roughly how long she stayed and which room was busiest. Which kind of processing explains this?
options: Effortful processing
Automatic processing
Deep processing of meaning
Prospective memory

why.correct: Information about time, space and frequency is often encoded without effort or intention. That is automatic processing.
options: Effortful processing needs attention and work, like studying vocabulary. She did not try to remember.
Right: Information about time, space and frequency is often encoded without effort or intention. That is automatic processing.
Deep processing means thinking about meaning on purpose. She did not study the evening.
Prospective memory is remembering to do something later, not noticing how long she stayed.

items.q: In rats, repeatedly stimulating a pathway in the hippocampus makes its synapses respond more strongly for weeks afterward, and blocking this change impairs learning. Which concept is this?
options: The all-or-none principle
Working memory
Long-term potentiation
Automatic processing

why.correct: A lasting increase in synaptic strength after repeated stimulation is long-term potentiation (LTP), thought to be a neural basis of learning and memory.
options: All-or-none describes a single neuron firing fully or not at all. It is not a lasting strengthening of synapses.
Working memory is the active workspace of short-term memory, a mental system, not a change in synapses.
Right: A lasting increase in synaptic strength after repeated stimulation is long-term potentiation (LTP), thought to be a neural basis of learning and memory.
Automatic processing is effortless encoding, a mental process, not a change at the synapse.

items.q: Put the stages of the multi-store model in the order information passes through them.
options: Sensory memory
Short-term memory
Long-term memory

why.correct: Input is held briefly in sensory memory; what is attended to moves to short-term memory; what is encoded there can be stored in long-term memory.

items.q: A patient with damage to the hippocampus cannot form new memories of events, yet over several days gets faster at tracing a star in a mirror without remembering ever practicing. What does this show?
options: Memory is stored in one single brain system, so the patient's impairment is mild
Procedural memory needs conscious awareness of each earlier practice session
Short-term memory is unaffected, so the practice is being held in sensory memory
Explicit and implicit memory depend partly on different brain systems

why.correct: The patient lost the ability to form new explicit memories (events) but still learned a skill (implicit, procedural memory). The two kinds of memory can come apart.
options: If one system stored everything, the skill could not improve while event memory failed.
The patient improved without remembering practicing, so the skill did not need conscious recall.
Sensory memory lasts seconds. Improvement over days shows lasting learning.
Right: The patient lost the ability to form new explicit memories (events) but still learned a skill (implicit, procedural memory). The two kinds of memory can come apart.
